overview.headline: How Congress turns bills into laws and how chambers differ

keyPoints.point: Congress serves as the lawmaking branch for federal government action
keyPoints.quote: Congress is the lawmaking branch of the federal government.

keyPoints.point: Bills move to a committee whose members research, discuss and make changes before a chamber vote
keyPoints.quote: Once a bill is introduced, it is assigned to a committee whose members will research, discuss, and make changes to the bill.

keyPoints.point: Both chambers vote on the same version of the bill after resolving differences
keyPoints.quote: Then both chambers vote on the same version of the bill.

keyPoints.point: A presidential veto can be overridden by Congress, but a pocket veto cannot be overridden
keyPoints.quote: This action is called a pocket veto, and it cannot be overridden by Congress.

keyPoints.point: The Senate and House show procedural differences in handling legislation and votes
keyPoints.quote: The Senate and the House have some procedural differences.

keyTerms.gloss: proposal for a new law that can change an existing law
keyTerms.quote: A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law.

keyTerms.gloss: group whose members research and discuss a bill and make changes
keyTerms.quote: Once a bill is introduced, it is assigned to a committee whose members will research, discuss, and make changes to the bill.

keyTerms.gloss: refuse to approve a bill when the president withholds signature
keyTerms.quote: Or the president can refuse to approve a bill. This is called a veto.

keyTerms.gloss: action called a pocket veto that cannot be overridden by Congress
keyTerms.quote: This action is called a pocket veto, and it cannot be overridden by Congress.

keyTerms.gloss: tax and revenue legislation that the House can initiate
keyTerms.quote: Only the House can initiate tax and revenue-related legislation
